title: Hubble image of M13's nucleus
caption: The core of globular cluster M13, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 13, NGC 6205 · constellation Hercules · about 25000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)

recognition.text: Published in the ESA/Hubble image archive. No published rating.

story: Many hundreds of thousands of stars crowd this Hubble view of the globular cluster M13, caught in a single instant as they move about. Among the globular clusters of the northern sky, M13 is one of the brightest and most familiar, and it is easy to find in the constellation of Hercules.

A globular cluster is a dense, ball-shaped swarm of old stars held together by gravity. Near the center the stars are packed especially closely, and Hubble's sharp vision can separate many of them into individual points of light.

This picture was not made from one observation. It is a composite of archival Hubble data from four separate science proposals, gathered with two Hubble cameras, WFPC2 and the Advanced Camera for Surveys. Broadband filters isolated light from the blue, visible and infrared parts of the spectrum.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.48 x 2.50 arcminutes) and distance (25000 light years), the frame spans roughly 18 × 18 light-years. Its light set out about 25,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This composite combines archival data from Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 and Advanced Camera for Surveys, through blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The color assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and Hubble's sharp view picks out individual stars in the crowded center.
